import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Ben Green's Open Problem 5

*References:*
- [Gr24] [Green, Ben. "100 open problems." (2024).](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.5)
- [BaSo85] Babai L, Sós VT. Sidon sets in groups and induced subgraphs of Cayley graphs.
  European Journal of Combinatorics. 1985 Jun 1;6(2):101-14.
- [Ke97] Kedlaya, K. S., *Large product-free subsets of finite groups*, J. Combin. Theory
  Ser. A 77 (1997), no. 2, 339–343.
- [Ke09] Kedlaya, K. S., *Product-free subsets of groups, then and now*, Contemp. Math., 479,
  American Mathematical Society, Providence, RI, 2009, 169–177.
- [Go08] Gowers, W. T., *Quasirandom groups*, Combin. Probab. Comput. 17 (2008), no. 3,
  363–387.
-/

open scoped MatrixGroups

local notation "SL₂" p => SL(2, ZMod p)

namespace Green5

/--
Which finite groups have the smallest biggest product-free sets?

We formalise this as: determine the supremum of exponents $\alpha$ such that every nontrivial
finite group of order $n$ contains a product-free set of size $\geq c n^{\alpha}$ for some
absolute constant $c > 0$. (The trivial group is excluded since its only product-free subset
is empty.) Kedlaya [Ke97] showed that $\alpha = 11/14$ is admissible, and Green suggests this
exponent may well be sharp; the candidate extremal family is the Ree groups ${}^2G_2(q)$,
$q = 3^{2m+1}$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 20]
theorem green_5 :
    IsLUB {α : ℝ | ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ (G : Type) [Group G] [Fintype G], Nontrivial G →
      ∃ S : Finset G, IsProductFree (S : Set G) ∧
        c * (Fintype.card G : ℝ) ^ α ≤ (S.card : ℝ)}
      answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
Kedlaya [Ke97] observed, refining some work of Babai and Sós [BaSo85], that it follows from the
classification of finite simple groups that every finite group $G$ of order $n$ has a
product-free subset of size $\gg n^{11/14}$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 20]
theorem green_5.variants.kedlaya :
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ (G : Type) [Group G] [Fintype G], Nontrivial G →
      ∃ S : Finset G, IsProductFree (S : Set G) ∧
        c * (Fintype.card G : ℝ) ^ ((11 : ℝ) / 14) ≤ (S.card : ℝ) := by
  sorry

-- TODO(theebayuser): implement Ree groups variant (candidate sharp example for `green_5`)

/--
A good model problem would be to determine the largest product-free subsets of
$\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 20]
theorem green_5.variants.sl_two (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] :
    let S : Finset (SL₂ p) := answer(sorry)
    MaximalFor (IsProductFree (M := SL₂ p)) Set.ncard (S : Set (SL₂ p)) := by
  sorry

/--
For the largest product-free subsets of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$ of order $n$, the
best-known upper bound is $O(n^{8/9})$, due to Gowers [Go08].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 20]
theorem green_5.variants.gowers_sl_two :
    ∃ C > (0 : ℝ), ∀ (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime], ∀ S : Finset (SL₂ p),
      IsProductFree (S : Set (SL₂ p)) →
      (S.card : ℝ) ≤ C * (Fintype.card (SL₂ p) : ℝ) ^ ((8 : ℝ) / 9) := by
  sorry

end Green5

findings.description: The main declaration requests only a real number: the supremum of exponents for a uniform lower bound on product-free-set size. It does not request or characterize any extremal groups or group families. Thus it captures the optimal-exponent aspect of the problem, but not literally the question of which groups have the smallest largest product-free sets. The supremum also forgets subpolynomial factors in extremal sizes. Green's comments make this a defensible quantitative interpretation, and the docstring explicitly acknowledges the choice, so this is a modelling concern rather than a definite misformalization. It is not, however, an established equivalent reformulation of the full qualitative question.
findings.source_evidence: Green, “100 open problems,” Problem 5, p. 4, asks “Which finite groups have the smallest biggest product-free sets?” The comments discuss sharpness of the exponent 11/14 and specifically propose the Ree groups as the potential extremal family. https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.5
findings.suggested_fix: Retain the current statement as an optimal-exponent variant. For the full extremal-group question, additionally request or characterize extremal group families and their matching bounds—for example, formalize the proposed Ree-family sharpness assertion along unbounded group orders. The maintainer should decide whether the intended scope is only the quantitative exponent question.

reformulations.difference: “Largest product-free subset” is expressed using MaximalFor IsProductFree Set.ncard on the set underlying an answer of type Finset (SL₂ p).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: MaximalFor includes product-freeness of the proposed set. Since cardinalities lie in the linear order ℕ, its maximality condition is equivalent to every competing product-free set having cardinality at most that of the answer. For prime p the ambient group is finite, so all competing sets correspond to finsets and Set.ncard equals their ordinary cardinality; its infinite-set default is unreachable. The full equivalence with product-freeness plus ∀ T : Finset G, IsProductFree ↑T → T.card ≤ S.card was proved in scratch.lean.

reformulations.difference: The source's O(n^(8/9)) upper bound on the largest product-free set is expressed as a single positive constant bounding every product-free finset for every prime, without a sufficiently-large-prime restriction.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Bounding the maximum size is equivalent to bounding every product-free subset in a finite group. An eventual O(n^(8/9)) bound extends to all primes by increasing the constant: only finitely many primes are exceptional, every subset has size at most n, and n is positive, so their ratios to n^(8/9) are bounded by the finite collection of values n^(1/9). Conversely, the global bound immediately implies the asymptotic one. This also accommodates the small primes 2 and 3.

review.notes: All four declarations, answer types/scopes, and underlying definitions were checked. No definite mathematical error was found in the three variants. Kedlaya's cited survey explicitly assumes n > 1, justifying Nontrivial G; Lean also confirmed Nontrivial G ↔ 1 < Fintype.card G. Scratch proofs establish that only the empty set is product-free in a trivial group, a singleton is product-free exactly when its element is not the identity, and the main exponent set is nonempty, downward closed, and bounded above, without using the reviewed sorry theorems. Computations gave |SL₂(F₂)| = 6, |SL₂(F₃)| = 24, |SL₂(F₅)| = 120, and maximum product-free size 3 for SL₂(F₂). The source retains the open status of Problem 5 and its model problem. Full copies of the 1985 and 1997 papers could not be retrieved; their relevant results were checked in the cited Kedlaya survey and Gowers introduction instead. Experiments are under /workspace/review/; the reviewed file was not modified.
